title: Checklist: Work, Money, Home and Family
summary: Employment, loans and tax, property and family rights - every point in simple words.
sectionRefs: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005

body.text: Part three of your checklist: your job, your money, your home and your family. These are the biggest things in most people's lives.

items: 77. Appointment letter. Read your job title, salary, work location, probation and conditions before you join.
78. Salary. Know your agreed salary, payment dates and lawful deductions.
79. Payslips and tax papers. Keep payslips, Form 16 and salary-credit bank statements.
80. Notice period. Understand the notice clause, any buy-out option, and how dues are settled.
81. Resignation. Follow the proper procedure and keep proof that you submitted it and it was acknowledged.
82. Termination. Know which contract terms and legal protections apply to your job.
83. Working hours and overtime. Check the rules on working time, overtime and rest.
84. Leave and holidays. Know your leave entitlements and the company policy.
85. Provident fund (PF). Know your EPF eligibility, contributions, UAN and transfer or withdrawal rules.
86. Gratuity. Understand when you are eligible and how it is calculated.
87. Maternity benefits. Know the maternity protections and eligibility rules.
88. Workplace sexual harassment. The POSH Act protects you; every workplace should have an Internal Committee.
89. Discrimination and retaliation. Know the protections that apply to your situation.
90. Employment documents. Keep your offer letter, contract, performance records and full-and-final settlement.
91. Work from home. Your work-from-home terms depend on the law, your contract and the circumstances.
92. Grievances. Know the right route: HR, the labour department, conciliation or a court.
93. Loan agreements. Understand the interest rate, processing fees, penalties, repayment schedule and foreclosure terms.
94. Loan defaults. Know what happens if you miss payments, and how collection works.
95. Recovery agents. They cannot threaten, abuse or invade your privacy to collect a loan.
96. Guarantor. A guarantor can be made to pay if the borrower defaults. Never sign casually.
97. Credit reports. Check your credit report for mistakes and dispute them with the lender.
98. Bank complaints. Use the bank's grievance process, then the RBI's complaint mechanism.
99. Unauthorised transactions. Tell your bank fast. How quickly you report affects your liability.
100. Credit cards. Understand interest, minimum payments, fees and billing disputes.
101. Income tax. Learn about taxable income, deductions, TDS and when you must file a return.
102. GST and bills. Know when GST applies and how to check an invoice.
103. Insurance. Read the exclusions, waiting periods and claim conditions.
104. Investments. Understand the risk, and beware of 'guaranteed returns'.
105. Nominees and inheritance. A nominee is not the same as an owner or heir.
106. Financial scams. Be careful of guaranteed returns and requests to pay into a personal account.
107. Property title. Verify ownership and the title documents before buying land or a house.
108. Encumbrances. Check for loans or claims on the property. No single certificate proves everything.
109. Registration and stamp duty. Understand the registration process and charges.
110. Rental agreements. Read the rent, deposit, maintenance, notice, termination and renewal clauses.
111. Security deposits. Know your rights on deductions and refunds.
112. Eviction. Follow the legal process. No one can just throw a tenant out.
113. Utilities and maintenance. Know who pays for electricity, water, common areas and repairs.
114. Inheritance. Learn the succession rules, wills and the value of ownership documents.
115. Neighbour disputes. There are remedies for encroachment, damage, nuisance and access problems.
116. Construction permissions. Check local approvals, building rules and land-use limits.
117. Land records. Learn how to check revenue and registration records in Tamil Nadu, and their limits.
118. Marriage. Understand the marriage law that applies, the conditions, registration and spouses' rights.
119. Divorce. Learn the grounds, the procedure and the consequences.
120. Maintenance. A spouse, child or parent may be entitled to maintenance if they cannot support themselves.
121. Domestic violence. The Domestic Violence Act, 2005 protects women from physical, emotional, sexual and economic abuse.
122. Sexual harassment. Know the criminal-law protections and workplace complaint procedure.
123. Stalking and intimidation. Know when behaviour becomes a crime, and how to report it.
124. Dowry. Giving, taking or demanding dowry is prohibited by law.
125. Child sexual abuse. The POCSO Act protects children; reporting is mandatory for many people.
126. Child marriage. The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act bans marriage below the legal age.
127. Child labour. There are restrictions and protections against children working in harmful jobs.
128. Adoption and guardianship. Follow the legal process, not informal arrangements.
129. Inheritance. Learn which personal law or succession rule applies to your family.
130. Senior citizens. The law protects older persons' maintenance and welfare.

body.text: Family matters involve sensitive facts and different personal laws. The exact position depends on your situation - check the law and get proper advice.
Keep every document: appointment letters, payslips, loan papers, rent agreements and property records. Papers win cases.

practicalSteps: Keep a folder (physical or on cloud) of all job, loan, rent and property papers.
Read every contract before signing, and ask for a copy.
For unpaid salary, complain to the Labour Commissioner; for PF, to the EPFO.
For family or domestic-violence help, call 181; for emergencies, call 112.
exceptions: Not every employee has the same rights - it depends on the job, wage level, establishment and state.
Inheritance and marriage rules differ by religion under the personal law that applies to you.

faqs.q: Can my landlord throw me out at once?
faqs.a: No. Eviction must follow the agreement and the law, with proper written notice and, if disputed, a court or Rent Authority order.

faqs.q: Is a nominee the same as an heir?
faqs.a: No. A nominee can receive the money, but ownership and inheritance are decided by succession law.

misconceptions.myth: A nominee becomes the owner of the money or property.
misconceptions.fact: A nominee only receives it. Who truly owns it is decided by succession law and any will.
